Hjernetumorer hos hunde, genetik og diagnostik
Patienter til studiet:
Til projektet inkluderes 20 hunde med styrket mistanke om hjernetumorer, hvor ejer har truffet den svære beslutning om aflivning. Hundene vil i forbindelse med aflivning få taget en blodprøve, og de vil efter aflivning få udtaget rygmarvsvæske, en biopsi af tumoren og en muskelbiopsi. Herefter vil de kunne kremeres, enten med eller uden urne, afhængigt af ejers ønske.
Formål med projektet:
Når en hund rammes af en hjernetumor, kan sygdommen komme til udtryk ved flere forskellige kliniske tegn, afhængigt af hvilken type tumor hunden lider af, og hvor i hjernen tumoren sidder.
Når en hund mistænkes for at lide af en hjernetumor, vil den få foretaget en grundig klinisk og neurologisk undersøgelse, samt få taget en række blodprøver. Disse undersøgelser har til formål at bestemme, om hundens problem stammer fra hjernen eller ej, altså om problemet er af intrakraniel eller ekstrakraniel oprindelse. Hvis ekstrakranielle årsager til hundens problem kan udelukkes, vil næste skridt i udredningsprocessen være en MR- eller CT-scanning af hjernen. På denne vil man i mange tilfælde kunne identificere strukturelle forandringer i hjernevævet, som kan indikere, at hundens problem er forsaget af en hjernetumor. Dog kræves en biopsi, hvis der skal stilles en endelig diagnose, hvilket ofte fravælges, og en sikker diagnose stilles derfor først efter aflivning.
På Universitetshospitalet for Familiedyr forsker vi netop nu i, om man med en blod- eller rygmarvsvæskeprøve kan karakterisere hjernetumorer hos hunde, og dermed potentielt gøre vejen fra mistanke til diagnose kortere.
DNA fra tumor-celler kan findes i kropsvæsker:
Når en tumorcelle dør, udskiller den små DNA-fragmenter til bl.a. blodbanen. Disse DNA-fragmenter, såkaldt cirkulerende tumor DNA (ctDNA), har de seneste år vakt massiv interesse inden for kræftforskningen. Da ctDNA direkte afspejler tumorens arvemasse, er håbet, at man i fremtiden vil kunne bruge ctDNA som markør til diagnostik og monitorering af kræftpatienter. Fænomenet kaldes en ’flydende biopsi’, og kan potentielt gøre en forskel for patienter med tumorer, der er vanskelige at bioptere på traditionel vis.
Om forskningsprojektet:
I dette projekt undersøges det, hvilke mutationer i arvematerialet der driver udviklingen af forskellige hjernetumorer hos hunde. Til dette formål anvendes hel-exom sekventering af både tumorvæv og rask referencevæv. Det undersøges desuden, om tumor-specifikke mutationer kan genfindes i blod og rygmarvsvæske ved ddPCR.
Hunde som deltager i projektet forventes at bidrage med vigtig ny viden til kræftforskningen, som potentielt vil kunne gøre en forskel for både hunde og mennesker med hjernetumorer i fremtiden.<\p>

Genetic Epilepsy in the Dog
Projektbeskrivelse og formål:
At karakterisere epilepsi hos Petit Basset Griffon Vendeen og Belgisk Hyrdehund samt at klarlægge forekomsten af lidelsen i de to racer. Såfremt en genetisk disponering kan påvises, vil videre undersøgelser omkring arveligheden eventuelt kunne resultere i information som kan belyse visse aspekter vedrørende arvelig epilepsi hos mennesker. I disse år er der stort fokus på at afklare den arvelige baggrund for mange forskellige sygdomme hos både mennesker og dyr. Hos hund anslås det, at cirka 1 % af hele hundebestanden på verdensbasis har epilepsi. Imidlertid findes der hunderacer, hvor forekomsten er mange gange højere end hos den generelle hundebestand. En hunderace er karakteriseret ved at bestå af mange individer, som ligner hinanden og deler den samme pulje af gener. De udgør derfor en meget ensartet bestand, når man ser på arvelige faktorer.
Epilepsi er den hyppigst forekommende lidelse i nervesystemet hos både hund og menneske og arvelige former for epilepsi ses hos begge. Epilepsi udvikles som følge af en forøget aktivitet i nervecellerne i hjernen, enten som følge af ændrede forhold i cellerne og deres funktion eller som følge af sygdomsprocesser i hjernen. Epilepsi udløses typisk ganske pludseligt og kortvarigt, og kan i mange tilfælde udtrykkes som kramper i hele eller dele af kroppen. Bevidstheden er ofte nedsat under anfaldene, som ligner hinanden fra gang til gang. Undersøgelser af arvelighed hos mennesker er vanskeliggjort af de mange år, der ligger mellem hver generation i en familie (cirka 30 år). Her har forskning i arvelig epilepsi hos hund en klar fordel i, at der kun er få år mellem hver generation (generationsintervallet er her cirka 2 år). Man kan således hurtigere undersøge mange generationer i en familie af hunde. På baggrund af ovenstående er undersøgelser af arvelig epilepsi hos specifikke hunderacer derfor en oplagt mulighed for at få informationer vedrørende både den molekylærgenetiske baggrund for epilepsi samt den vævsmæssige defekt, som fører til epileptiske anfald. Resultater af sådanne undersøgelser kan i fremtiden være til stor gavn både hunde og mennesker.
Patienter til studiet:
Alle hunde med mulig epilepsi af racerne Petit Basset Griffon Vendeen og Belgisk Hyrdehund, varianterne Groenendael og Tervueren, kunne indgå i projektet. Det er dog foreløbigt afsluttet og indtaget af patienter lukket pr. 1.1.2011.

Fluorescentie Levensduur Beeldvorming
Een nieuwe beeldvormingstechniek om chirurgen te begeleiden bij het verwijderen van kanker: Fluorescentie Levensduur Beeldvorming
(S. Janssen/H. de Rooster)
An English version of this information for owners/veterinarians can be found later in this document
Honden en katten waarbij kanker in een vroeg stadium wordt vastgesteld krijgen vaak de optie chirurgie aangeboden. Dit blijft een van de beste mogelijke behandelingen voor kankerpatiënten waarbij nog geen uitzaaiingen worden waargenomen. Tijdens de chirurgie proberen chirurgen de volledige massa te verwijderen om de kans op recidieven te verkleinen. Omdat chirurgen tijdens heelkundige ingrepen aangewezen zijn op hun eigen zicht en tast,
én ons zicht niet toelaat om alle kleine kanker cellen te detecteren, wordt er gezocht naar nieuwe technieken die chirurgen kunnen helpen. Er worden contrast stoffen ontwikkeld die als kleine gidsjes de kanker cellen zichtbaar maken die we niet met het blote oog kunnen zien. De contraststoffen doen dit door licht uit te zenden. Dat licht kan dan gedetecteerd worden met speciale camera systemen. Deze techniek wordt ‘Fluorescentie-geleide chirurgie’ genoemd.
Ondanks deze goede vooruitgang, komt het toch nog redelijk vaak voor dat een contraststof zich ergens anders bevindt dan enkel ter hoogte van het kanker weefsel. In deze studie willen we een nieuwe beeldvormingstechniek gebruiken tijdens chirurgie om na te gaan of deze chirurgen beter kan helpen om een onderscheid te maken tussen de aanwezige contraststof ter hoogte van de kankercellen en de aanwezigheid van de contraststof op andere plekken (zoals in ontstekingsweefsel). Dit is mogelijk door te focussen op de cellulaire omgeving van de contraststof. Deze techniek noemen we ‘Fluorescentie Levensduur Beeldvorming’ of ‘Fluorescence Lifetime Imaging’.
WAT IS FLUORESCENTIE LEVENSDUUR BEELDVORMING?
Om uit te leggen wat Fluorescentie Levensduur Beeldvorming inhoudt, moet eerst de term ‘Fluorescentie’ gedefinieerd worden. Fluorescentie is de fysische eigenschap van een molecule of contraststof om licht van een bepaalde golflengte te absorberen en weer uit te zenden. Met Fluorescentie Beeldvorming meten we de hoeveelheid licht die wordt uitgezonden door de contraststof. Fluorescentie Levensduur Beeldvorming daarentegen richt zich niet op hoeveel licht wordt uitgezonden, maar focust zich eerder op de tijd die de molecule nodig heeft om dit licht uit te zenden. Deze tijd is zeer kort (kleiner dan 1 nanoseconde) en afhankelijk van de omgeving waarin een molecule of contraststof zich bevindt. Daardoor wordt het mogelijk gemaakt om de aanwezigheid van de contraststof in een tumor te onderscheiden van de aanwezigheid van een contraststof in gezond weefsel.
WAT IS HET DOEL VAN DEZE STUDIE?
Dankzij veelbelovende resultaten van onze preklinische studies met Fluorescentie Levensduur Beeldvorming kunnen we nu starten met een klinische studie bij honden en katten. Elke patiënt die ingepland wordt voor chirurgische verwijdering van een tumor en waarbij een bijkomende marge aan gezond weefsel wordt verwijderd volgens standaard chirurgische protocollen kan deelnemen aan de studie. In deze studie willen we bevestigen of het gebruik van deze beeldvormingstechniek tijdens chirurgie een toegevoegde waarde biedt in het volledig verwijderen van de kanker ten opzichte van huidige Fluorescentie Beeldvorming technieken. In deze studie gebruiken we de contrast stof ‘Indocyanine Green’ die reeds goed gekeurd is voor verschillende toepassingen in zowel de diergeneeskunde als humane geneeskunde door het Europees Geneesmiddelen Agenschap.
Meer info voor dierenartsen
English version for owners
English version for vets
DEELNAME AAN PROJECT
Bij deelname aan deze studie zal uw hond of kat met kanker - die reeds werd ingepland voor chirurgie of waarvoor chirurgie ingepland zal worden - toegang krijgen tot een nieuwe beeldvormingstechniek om de kans op volledige verwijdering van de kanker te verhogen. Daarnaast krijgt uw huisdier als een van de eerste toegang tot een veelbelovende toepassing die pas later beschikbaar zal komen voor mensen.
Voor deze studie dient uw huisdier de dag voorafgaand aan de chirurgie nuchter naar de faculteit te komen. Omdat de contraststof die gebruikt wordt 24 uur nodig heeft om te lokaliseren ter hoogte van de tumor zal de patiënt deze een dag van te voren toegediend krijgen. Hierna kan uw lieve viervoeter met u mee naar huis of kan deze gehospitaliseerd worden. Afhankelijk van uw keuze, meldt u zich de volgende dag aan bij  de dienst chirurgie voor de verwijdering van de massa of komt u naar de faculteit na de chirurgie. Tijdens en na de chirurgie zullen een paar beelden genomen worden van de massa en het wondbed na verwijdering van de massa.
TEGEMOETKOMING VOOR DEELNAME
Bij deelname aan deze studie wordt de pathologische beoordeling van de massa na de chirurgie vergoedt door het project. De resultaten van de pathologie worden zodra beschikbaar gedeeld met u en uw dierenarts. Er worden geen bijkomende kosten gemaakt vergeleken met andere patiënten die zich aanbieden bij de dienst chirurgie en niet mee doen aan de klinische studie.
Uw deelname aan deze studie zal ons belangrijke informatie opleveren met betrekking tot het gebruik van fluorescentie levensduur beeldvorming voor intra-operatieve begeleiding van chirurgen tijdens kanker resectie.

title: PRISM: radiation-treatment access and funded follow-up for canine glioma
current_primary_text:
PRISM Trial: Precision Research Integrating Symptoms and Molecular Biology in Canine Glioma
STATUS: Active - Recruiting
High-grade gliomas are aggressive brain tumors that are difficult to treat in dogs. While surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy may help some dogs, we still have much to learn about why some tumors respond better to treatment than others.
The purpose of this study is to better understand brain tumors in dogs by collecting information about each dog's health, MRI findings, tumor characteristics, and in some dogs, how they respond to radiation treatment. By
studying many dogs with naturally occurring brain tumors
, we hope to identify patterns that will help veterinarians diagnose these tumors more accurately, predict how they may behave, and develop more effective treatments in the future.
Although participation in this study may not directly benefit every dog, the information gained will help improve the care of dogs diagnosed with brain tumors and advance the development of new treatment options. Every dog that participates helps us learn more about brain tumors and brings us one step closer to improving treatment and quality of life for future dogs facing this disease.
INVESTIGATOR: Christine Toedebusch, DVM, PhD, DACVIM, Associate Professor

Current Clinical Trials
Current Clinical Trials
We are currently seeking patients for enrollment in funded oncology clinical trials. Study goals and suitability for each patient are discussed in detail with the clients prior to enrollment. Although clinical trial enrollment may not be the best option for all patients, in many cases, clinical trial participation provides the opportunity to receive novel, cutting-edge therapies free of charge or at a reduced cost and may facilitate treatment of pets where it would not otherwise be possible due to financial constraints or lack of other therapy options. Criteria for enrollment are outlined for each tumor type below. Please direct referrals or questions to the Oncology Clinical Trials Service at 573-882-7821.
Current Trials and Studies
Bruton’s Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitor (BI705564) for Canine B‑Cell Lymphoma
The University of Missouri Veterinary Health Center is enrolling dogs in a clinical trial evaluating an investigational oral Bruton’s Tyrosine Kinase (BTK) inhibitor—
BI705564
—for the treatment of newly diagnosed B‑cell lymphoma. This exploratory, multicenter field study aims to assess both
efficacy
and
safety
of BTK inhibition in canine patients.
Eligibility includes:
Dogs
>1 year old
and
10–50 kg
in body weight
Naïve
, untreated B‑cell lymphoma confirmed by cytology or histology with immunophenotyping (flow cytometry)
At least
two peripheral lymph nodes ≥2 cm
in longest diameter
WHO stage
II, III, or IV
B‑cell lymphoma
Adequate organ function on bloodwork and urinalysis
Performance score of
0–1
(normal to mildly decreased activity) and
life expectancy ≥1 month
Owner consent
Key exclusions:
T‑cell lymphoma
or involvement of skin, GI tract, or nervous system
Internal‑only disease (mediastinum, liver, spleen) without peripheral lymph node enlargement
Prior lymphoma treatment (chemotherapy, Tanovea, Laverdia, radiation) or long‑term corticosteroids (>2 weeks)
Hypercalcemia, MDR1 deficiency, pregnancy/lactation, or concurrent trial enrollment
Study overview:
Dogs will receive
oral BI705564 once daily for 3 months (84 days)
at
5 mg/kg
, with possible dose escalation to
10 mg/kg
in certain cases depending on early target occupancy results.
The study includes scheduled evaluations such as:
Physical examinations and lymph node measurements
Quality‑of‑life assessments
Bloodwork (CBC, chemistry, lymphoma testing)
Lymph node aspirates for
target occupancy
evaluation
Thoracic radiographs and abdominal ultrasound at screening
Follow‑up continues regularly throughout the 12‑week treatment period.
Potential benefits:
Access to a novel investigational BTK inhibitor designed to target B‑cell lymphoma
All

current_primary_text:
​最新消息-
總院
總院
2025年9月3日
招募犬黑色素瘤及骨肉瘤臨床試驗
招募犬黑色素瘤及骨肉瘤臨床試驗
台北長青動物醫院總院正在招募罹患
黑色素瘤(melanoma)或骨肉瘤(oesteosarcoma)
的狗參與臨床試驗！
此次的試驗是將IL15透過噴霧治療形式進行治療。IL15是一種細胞激素，具有促進免疫與抑制腫瘤生長的效果。
有許多人類腫瘤臨床試驗顯示IL-15具有治療腫瘤的潛力，此種藥物最近也被應用在狗的黑色素瘤及骨肉瘤，初步結果指出IL-15對這類患犬同樣具有治療效益。
試驗目的在於進一步驗證IL15 對於犬黑色素瘤及骨肉瘤長期控制的效果。
關於這個試驗的重點Q&A
1.這項治療的原理是什麼？
IL-15是一種細胞激素，能夠刺激自身的免疫細胞（NK細胞、T細胞）對抗腫瘤的生長和轉移。
2.參加試驗的狗須符合哪些條件
a.經細胞學或組織病理學確診罹患
黑色素瘤或骨肉瘤
。b.患犬品種、年齡、體重、性別不限。c.肺部轉移病灶直徑需大於1.0公分。d.患犬沒有出現危及生命的腫瘤相關症狀。e.目前沒有使用類固醇或其他免疫抑制劑。f. 飼主須能配合每周回診治療追蹤，療程約10~12週。
3.治療過程是如何進行？
IL15藥劑以皮下注射方式給藥。若有肺部腫瘤轉移則會將藥劑放置在噴霧機內，患犬在清醒的狀態下佩戴呼吸面罩，含有藥劑的噴霧會隨著呼吸進入狗的肺部。
4.多久需回診一次？
每週治療一次，共八次治療。治療結束後�兩週需回診追蹤療效。
5.治療過程中需要進行哪些檢驗？治療前
需進行血檢、尿檢、X光或電腦斷層確認腫瘤狀態。
治療當日
需抽血檢查。
療程結束
後會再次進行血檢、尿檢、X光或電腦斷層評估效果。
6.參加這項試驗的狗可能有什麼副作用？
初步的研究顯示腫瘤患犬使用IL15可能發生的副作用為
疲倦、嗜睡、肝指數上升、下痢、呼吸加快
等，大多數情況下這類副作用並不會危及生命，可自行緩解。
7.參加這項試驗對我的狗有什麼好處？
先前的臨床試驗顯示IL15可以讓部分患犬的腫瘤縮小或消失，參加此次試驗的狗可能達到類似的效果。相較於傳統的血管注射化療，副作用的發生機率與嚴重程度較低。
8.參加試驗需要費用嗎？
此次試驗的IL15藥劑不收費，治療過程中所需的檢查及輔助用藥費用需由飼主自行負擔。

title: Pilot clinical trial of trametinib treatment in dogs with acute myeloid leukemia (AML)
current_primary_text:
Pilot clinical trial of anti-cancer therapy with trametinib in naturally occurring acute myeloid leukemia
STATUS: Active - Recruiting
Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a fast-growing cancer of the blood and bone marrow that affects both people and dogs. Dogs diagnosed with AML usually have a poor outlook, and current treatments only extend survival for a short time, typically about 1–2 months.
Researchers are looking for better treatment options for dogs with AML. Many dogs with AML have changes (mutations) in a gene called
NRAS
, which can cause cancer cells to grow and survive. This study is testing a medication called
trametinib
, which blocks signals that cancer cells use to grow.
The purpose of this study is to find out whether trametinib is safe for dogs with AML and whether it may help slow down or reduce the cancer. Information learned from this study may also help researchers better understand leukemia in people.
This trial is being led by the Clinical Hematopathology Laboratory in partnership with the Flint Animal Cancer Center of the Colorado State University Veterinary Health System and is sponsored by the Lutsen Linder Research Fund for Extremely Gorgeous Dogs.

title: Immunotherapy for canine oral melanoma
current_primary_text:
Immunotherapy for canine oral melanoma
Immunotherapy for canine oral melanoma
Oral melanoma is a highly aggressive disease with poor outcomes and no effective treatments. Our recent research has shown that a weakened form of the lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) is safe, and can trigger strong anti-tumor effects.
By injecting a small amount of this weakened virus directly into the tumor, we aim to activate the dog's immune system to fight the cancer. Additionally, we will collect and expand immune cells from the tumor, as these cells are more likely to recognize and attack cancer cells. These enhanced immune cells will then be reinfused into the patient to target existing or potential metastatic disease.
To evaluate our therapy, we will first perform a tumor biopsy to confirm the diagnosis and analyze the immune cells already present (Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes). We will then inject the tumor with the weakened virus. One week later, the tumor will be surgically removed, and immune cells from the cancer will be expanded for future use if metastases are present or develop later. After treatment, we will closely monitor the patients through periodic blood tests and imaging (CT scans) every three months.
A small group of dogs (randomly selected) will be the control, and while not receiving the virus injection, they will have their immune cells extracted from the tumor and expanded to be reinfused in case of progressive disease.
Client Compensation:
Cost of tumor biopsy, two CT imaging sessions, trial-related blood work, the viral reagent and injections, the collection priming and reinjection of the immune cells. Additionally, participating dogs are eligible to receive a $800 post-trial incentive.
Potential Medical Benefits:
Potential medical benefits include longer clinical remissions after surgical removal of the primary tumor, slowing down or remission of metastatic disease.
Potential Medical Risks:
Following tumor biopsy: bleeding, infection of the tumor, swelling, redness, pain, fever, and/or discharge/pus/odor at the biopsy site.
Following virus injection and reinfusion of immune cells, skin rash, fever, lethargy, and anaphylaxis.
What qualifies my pet for enrollment?
Inclusion Criteria:
Dogs that are otherwise healthy with localized cytologically or histologically confirmed oral melanoma will be recruited to the study.
Tumors need to be easily accessible to percutaneous injection and needle biopsy.
Exclusion Criteria:
Dogs with a history of immune deficiency or requiring immunosuppressive medications will be excluded.
A dog that received local radiation therapy to the primary tumor before trial enrolment will be excluded.
Diagnosis/Condition Being Studied:
Oral melanoma
Intervention to Be Studied:
Injection of weakened virus into the tumor and transfusion of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes

Combination therapy for dogs with Hemangiosarcoma
The objective of this study is to investigate the effectiveness of combining doxorubicin or carboplatin and temozolomide with propranolol in dogs with hemangiosarcoma. title: Molecularly targeted cytotoxin therapy by convection-enhanced delivery for canine glioma
current_primary_text:
Targeted chemotherapy for brain tumors in dogs
Targeted chemotherapy for glioma brain tumors in dogs
Principal Investigator
Bio Item
John H. Rossmeisl, Jr., DVM, MS, DACVIM–Internal Medicine, Neurology
, bio
Contact
jrossmei@vt.edu
Purpose
To determine the safety and effectiveness of a new chemotherapy drug and drug delivery method in the treatment of brain tumors (gliomas) in dogs.
Background
Both dogs and humans can develop brain tumors. In dogs, a type of tumor called a glioma is one of the most common brain tumors, and also one of the hardest to treat. Sadly, even with treatment, people and dogs with gliomas usually don’t live very long, and there is no cure. Current therapies aim to help patients with gliomas live longer and improve their quality of life.
In this clinical trial, we are testing the safety and effectiveness of molecularly targeted cytotoxins, a kind of chemotherapy, delivered directly to the patient's brain tumor. Developed by researchers at the
Thomas K. Hearn Brain Tumor Research Center
at the Wake Forest School of Medicine, the unique chemotherapy drugs used in this trial are designed to affect only cancer cells, and not normal brain tissue.
Earlier generations of these drugs have been used safely and effectively in dogs with gliomas.
Using special catheter tubes, the drug is infused directly into the tumor over a few hours. The drug treatment is monitored continuously with MRI to allow the research team to precisely track the drug delivery.
Eligibility
Dogs of any age, breed, or sex weighing between 3 and 45 kilograms (approximately 7-100 lbs.).
Dogs with mild to moderate neurological issues, related to their brain tumor.
Brain MRI scan should show a single mass in the brain with the characteristics of a glioma.
The tumor must measure at least 1 centimeter in diameter.
Dogs should not have any other significant health problems besides their brain tumor.
Exclusion Criteria
Dogs not expected to live through the initial treatment because of how sick they are and/or how fast their tumor is growing.
Dogs that have received immunotherapy in the last 6 months.
Dogs that have received chemotherapy in the last 6 weeks.
Dogs that have had surgery in the last 6 weeks.
Dogs that have had radiation therapy.
Dogs with seizures that can’t be controlled with medication.
Dogs currently diagnosed with any other type of cancer, in addition to their brain tumor.
Dogs experiencing any other illness or significant health problem.
Dogs who’ve had complications from anesthesia in the past.
Dogs with more than one brain tumor, or whose brain tumor has spread to more than one part of their brain.

The treatment administered in the trial involves a procedure that delivers chemotherapy directly to the patient’s brain tumor. title: Smart-Start therapy before CHOP for canine B-cell lymphoma
current_primary_text:
Breadcrumb
CVM
Hospitals
Clinical Trials
Smart-Start Therapy for Canine B-Cell Lymphoma
Canine
Lymphoma is one of the most common cancers we see in dogs. The current standard treatment — a combination chemotherapy protocol called CHOP — has been used for decades and can put most dogs into remission. Unfortunately, the cancer usually comes back within 6 to 12 months, and once it returns, it becomes much harder to treat.
We also know that CHOP has real drawbacks for families and their dogs: It's a big commitment. Treatment represents a significant financial investment and requires frequent visits to the veterinary hospital over several months.
Side effects can happen. Most dogs tolerate chemotherapy well, but some experience side effects that affect their quality of life.
Results haven't improved much over time. Despite years of use, survival times with CHOP have stayed roughly the same.
Perhaps most importantly, every dog currently receives the same chemotherapy — even though we know lymphoma doesn't behave the same way in every patient.
This study takes a more personalized path. By looking closely at the unique biology of each dog's cancer — including the environment surrounding the tumor cells — we can better understand why some dogs respond well to treatment and others don't. We then use that information to guide a "Smart-Start" treatment strategy, matching each dog with the therapy most likely to help them from the very beginning.
Our goals are twofold:
Get better results from the treatments we already have by choosing the right approach for each individual dog.
Build the foundation for the next generation of lymphoma care — treatments that target the specific biology of the cancer and, over time, rely less on traditional chemotherapy.
We hope this is a step toward smarter, more individualized cancer care for dogs — with the hope of longer, healthier remissions and a gentler treatment experience along the way.
Eligibility:
Dogs seen by the Cornell University Hospital for Animals (CUHA) who have been diagnosed with B-cell lymphoma, have had no prior treatment other than prednisolone, and are willing to pursue standard of care chemotherapy are eligible.

High Intensity Focused Ultrasound (HIFU) for Lymphoma in Dogs
Principal Investigators
Dr. Nick Dervisis, Associate Professor, Oncology
Dr. Michael Childress, Professor, Comparative Oncology
Background
Lymphoma is one of the most common cancers in dogs, and while chemotherapy can often put the disease into remission, it is rarely curative. This study is investigating whether a noninvasive technology, High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound (HIFU), can safely destroy part of a cancerous lymph node and stimulate the immune system to help fight the cancer throughout the body.
HIFU uses precisely focused ultrasound energy to generate heat that kills cancer cells within a targeted region, without surgery or radiation. Beyond directly killing tumor cells, this process may release tumor antigens and danger signals, "waking up" the immune system to recognize and attack lymphoma cells wherever they are.
In this trial, we will treat one enlarged lymph node with HIFU in dogs who have not yet received chemotherapy. We will then carefully analyze changes in the treated lymph node, an untreated lymph node, and the blood to see if the immune system is activated. All dogs will then receive a full course of standard CHOP chemotherapy at Purdue.
The potential benefits for participating dogs include receiving an innovative treatment at no cost, which may improve the effectiveness of chemotherapy and potentially help the immune system keep the cancer under control longer. There are no placebos in this trial.
Eligibility for Dogs to Participate in the Study
Be at least 1 year old and weigh over 8 kg (~18 lb)
Have an untreated, newly confirmed diagnosis of intermediate or large-cell, multicentric lymphoma (B or T-cell)
Have not received any chemotherapy, corticosteroids, or other anti-cancer treatment in the past 3 weeks (2 weeks for steroids)
Be healthy enough for sedation/anesthesia
Have completed full clinical staging (physical exam, lab work, imaging, and lymph node biopsy)
Have no other serious life-limiting diseases
Exclusion Criteria
Small-cell lymphoma or other round cell tumors
Stage V lymphoma (bone marrow or blood involvement) or extranodal lymphoma
Significant liver or kidney dysfunction
Poor overall performance status (VCOG > 2)
What is involved for the dog/dog owner?
Screening and Baseline Testing:
Owners will first meet with our oncology team to discuss standard treatment options. If interested in the trial, dogs will undergo:
Physical exam, CBC, chemistry, urinalysis
Thoracic radiographs and abdominal ultrasound
Lymph node biopsy (histopathology, immunohistochemistry, flow cytometry)
Clonality testing (PARR)
Study Procedures:
Day 0 (Baseline Sampling):
Needle biopsy of a lymph node on the opposite side of the biopsied lymph node
Blood draw for extracellular vesicle (EV) analysis
HIFU Treatment:
Within 1-7 days of baseline sampling, a portion of the target lymph node will be thermally ablated using the Theraclion Echopulse HIFU system under sedation.
Post-Treatment Sampling:
5-7 days after HIFU: repeat needle biopsies of treated and untreated lymph nodes and blood collection
Chemotherapy:
CHOP-based UW-25 protocol will begin immediately after post-HIFU sampling and continue for 25 weeks
Follow-Up:
Regular rechecks during chemotherapy for monitoring bloodwork and treatment response
Long-term monitoring until relapse
Financial Support
Once enrolled, the following will be provided at no cost:
The HIFU procedure, including sedation/anesthesia
All biopsies, blood tests, and lab work required by the study
A $2,000 credit toward the cost of the CHOP chemotherapy protocol
Up to $2,000 in additional support for managing any side effects linked to HIFU, or to be applied toward CHOP therapy
Reduced pricing ("research rate") for all other treatments and follow-up visits
Owners will be responsible for costs related to:
Initial diagnostic workup prior to enrollment
Any unrelated to HIFU medical care
Emergency visits due to HIFU

H-FIRE Liver Cancer Study
Principal Investigators
Dr. Nick Dervisis, Associate Professor, Oncology
Study Overview
This clinical trial is evaluating the safety and immune effects of High-Frequency Irreversible Electroporation (H-FIRE) for dogs diagnosed with liver cancer. While surgical removal of liver tumors can lead to excellent outcomes in selected cases, dogs with non-resectable or advanced disease currently have very limited treatment options and poor prognosis. H-FIRE is a novel, image-guided, non-thermal tumor ablation technology that delivers high-frequency electrical pulses to create microscopic pores in cancer cell membranes, leading to tumor cell death and potential immune activation.
Purpose of the Study
The goals of this study are to evaluate the safety and feasibility of H-FIRE in dogs with liver cancer, measure local and systemic immune responses after H-FIRE treatment, analyze tumor biopsies, blood immune cells, and cytokines before and after treatment, and determine whether a single H-FIRE treatment can stimulate a meaningful anti-tumor immune response.
Eligibility - Inclusion Criteria
Before enrollment, standard diagnostic testing is required, including:
Complete physical examination
Bloodwork (CBC and chemistry)
Urinalysis
Contrast CT scan of the chest and abdomen (under anesthesia or sedation)
Ultrasound-guided liver tumor biopsy
Dogs may qualify if:
One or more liver tumors are identified
Tumors are amenable to surgical resection
The dog is a suitable candidate for anesthesia and surgery
The owner has reviewed all standard-of-care options and elects to participate
Eligibility - Exclusion Criteria
Dogs are not eligible if they have:
Severe systemic illness that prevents safe anesthesia or surgery
Coagulation disorders that prevent biopsy or electroporation
Medical conditions that substantially increase anesthetic risk
Owner declines surgical tumor removal following H-FIRE
What Participation Involves
H-FIRE Treatment:
The H-FIRE procedure is performed under general anesthesia and guided by ultrasound. One or more needle electrodes are placed through a 1-2 mm skin opening into the tumor. Electrical pulses are delivered in microsecond bursts. Total treatment time is typically under 30 minutes.
Surgery (5-7 Days Later):
Surgical removal of the liver tumor under general anesthesia with a CT scan obtained immediately before surgery.
Follow-Up:
Dogs return at 2 weeks post-surgery for physical examination and suture removal. Additional diagnostics may be performed if medically indicated.
Risks and Side Effects
H-FIRE is an experimental therapy and is not part of standard veterinary care. Potential risks include fever, tumor inflammation, tumor-site discomfort, systemic inflammation, severe infection, and death. Diagnostic and anesthesia risks include bruising, inflammation, infection, anesthetic reactions, cardiopulmonary complications, and rare death.
Potential Benefits
Your dog may or may not directly benefit. Potential benefits include partial financial support for treatment, access to a novel tumor-targeted therapy, possible local tumor destruction, possible immune activation, and contribution to research benefiting both dogs and humans.
Alternatives to Participation
Alternatives include surgery alone, palliative medical management, no treatment, or euthanasia when medically appropriate.
One-Sentence Financial Summary
The study provides a $2,000 surgical credit and covers all H-FIRE, recheck, and post H-FIRE CT costs; owners remain responsible for remaining surgical fees, complications, and unrelated medical care.
Costs and Compensation
Covered by the Study:
$2,000 credit toward surgical resection
100% of H-FIRE procedure costs (anesthesia, electrodes, treatment delivery, side-effect management)
100% of post-H-FIRE CT imaging
100% of recheck visit costs
Owner Responsibility:
Remaining surgical costs beyond the $2,000 credit
Any medical complications unrelated to H-FIRE therapy
Any medical care not required by the study
Any unrelated medical expenses
Typical surgical cost at Purdue ranges between $4,000-$8,000 depending on tumor location and surgical complexity.
Voluntary Participation and Withdrawal
Participation is entirely voluntary. Owners may withdraw their dog from the study at any time without affecting access to standard care. Dogs may also be withdrawn for medical or safety reasons. Samples collected before withdrawal may still be used unless the owner requests otherwise.
Confidentiality
All study data are confidential. Published results will not include identifying information. Research records are stored securely and accessible only to authorized personnel.

HIFU Osteosarcoma Study
Principal Investigators
Dr. Nick Dervisis, Associate Professor, Oncology
Dr. Michael Childress, Professor, Comparative Oncology
Study Overview
This clinical trial evaluates the safety, feasibility, and biological impact of High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound (HIFU) for dogs newly diagnosed with appendicular osteosarcoma (OSA). Osteosarcoma is an aggressive primary bone cancer with a high risk of lung metastasis even with current standard treatments. HIFU is a noninvasive, image-guided technology that uses focuses ultrasound energy to generate heat and destroy targeted tumor tissue without skin incision.
Purpose of the Study
The goal of this study is to determine whether HIFU can safely modulate the tumor microenvironment, stimulate immune responses, and enhance future combinations with immune-based therapies. Advanced functional imaging and molecular analysis will be used to characterize biological effects before and after HIFU treatment.
Eligibility - Inclusion Criteria
At least 1 year old and >8 kg (18 lb)
Confirmed appendicular osteosarcoma
No evidence of metastatic disease
Suitable acoustic window for HIFU
Healthy enough for anesthesia and surgery
No chemotherapy within 3 weeks and no corticosteroids within 2 weeks
No other serious life-limiting disease
Relatively normal organ function
Eligibility - Exclusion Criteria
Other cancer types or metastatic osteosarcoma
No acoustic access to the tumor for HIFU
Other life-limiting illness
Poor overall performance status (VCOG _ 2)
What Participation Involves
Screening and baseline evaluation include physical examination, bloodwork, CT imaging, biopsy, and ultrasound assessment of tumor accessibility. On Day 0, dogs undergo functional imaging (Dynamic Contrast CT and Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy). On Day 1, partial tumor ablation is performed using HIFU under general anesthesia. Five to seven days later, repeat imaging and sample collection are performed. Between Days 6-8, standard-of-care limb amputation is performed. After recovery, dogs receive adjuvant carboplatin chemotherapy.
Follow-Up
After surgery and recovery (approximately 14 days), dogs begin standard carboplatin chemotherapy. Following the completion of chemotherapy, dogs return every 3 months for re-staging, ideally with CT imaging of the chest and abdomen. Owners are asked to notify the oncology team of any changes in their pet's health.
Risks
HIFU risks may include skin irritation, swelling, increased pain at the treatment site, unknown risk of bone fracture, systemic inflammation, abscess formation, and in rare cases, death. Diagnostic procedures may cause bruising, inflammation, or infection. General anesthesia carries small risks, including rare fatal complications.
Chemotherapy is not experimental but may cause vomiting, diarrhea, loss of appetite, and decreased blood cell counts. Dogs will be monitored carefully and supported as needed.
Potential Benefits
Your dog may or may not directly benefit from participation. Potential benefits include access to a novel noninvasive tumor ablation therapy, advanced imaging and molecular tumor analysis, partial financial assistance for surgery, and contribution to research benefiting both dogs and humans.
Alternatives
Alternatives to participation include standard limb amputation followed by chemotherapy alone, palliative care, no treatment, or euthanasia when medically appropriate.
One-Sentence Financial Summary
The study fully covers all HIFU and functional imaging costs, provides up to $2,600 toward surgical amputation, and covers chemotherapy recheck visits, while owners remain responsible for remaining surgery, chemotherapy, and surgery-related complication costs.
Costs and Compensation
Covered by the Study:
100% of all HIFU-related costs (general anesthesia, samples, treatment, management of HIFU-related side effects)
100% of all functional imaging (Dynamic Contrast CT and Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy)
Up to $2,600 toward surgical amputation
Free recheck visits during chemotherapy
Owner Responsibility:
Initial diagnostics and staging
Remaining surgical costs beyond the $2,600 credit
Chemotherapy drug administration (carboplatin)
Any medical complications related to surgery
Any unrelated medical care
Total expected cost of surgery and chemotherapy typically ranges from $4,000-$6,000 depending on dog size, limb affected, tumor location, and surgical complexity.
Voluntary Participation and Withdrawal
Participation is voluntary. Owners may withdraw at any time. Withdrawing does not affect access to care. Samples already collected may still be used unless the owner requests otherwise.
Confidentiality
All information collected during this study is confidential. Research records are secured, and published results will not contain personally identifying information.

On Day 0, dogs undergo functional imaging (Dynamic Contrast CT and Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy). On Day 1, partial tumor ablation is performed using HIFU under general anesthesia. Five to seven days later, repeat imaging and sample collection are performed. Between Days 6-8, standard-of-care limb amputation is performed. After recovery, dogs receive adjuvant carboplatin chemotherapy.
Follow-Up
After surgery and recovery (approximately 14 days), dogs begin standard carboplatin chemotherapy. Following the completion of chemotherapy, dogs return every 3 months for re-staging, ideally with CT imaging of the chest and abdomen. Owners are asked to notify the oncology team of any changes in their pet's health.
Risks
HIFU risks may include skin irritation, swelling, increased pain at the treatment site, unknown risk of bone fracture, systemic inflammation, abscess formation, and in rare cases, death. Diagnostic procedures may cause bruising, inflammation, or infection. General anesthesia carries small risks, including rare fatal complications.
Chemotherapy is not experimental but may cause vomiting, diarrhea, loss of appetite, and decreased blood cell counts. Dogs will be monitored carefully and supported as needed.
Potential Benefits
Your dog may or may not directly benefit from participation. Potential benefits include access to a novel noninvasive tumor ablation therapy, advanced imaging and molecular tumor analysis, partial financial assistance for surgery, and contribution to research benefiting both dogs and humans.
Alternatives
Alternatives to participation include standard limb amputation followed by chemotherapy alone, palliative care, no treatment, or euthanasia when medically appropriate.
One-Sentence Financial Summary
The study fully covers all HIFU and functional imaging costs, provides up to $2,600 toward surgical amputation, and covers chemotherapy recheck visits, while owners remain responsible for remaining surgery, chemotherapy, and surgery-related complication costs.

High Intensity Focused Ultrasound (HIFU) for Lymphoma in Dogs
Principal Investigators
Dr. Nick Dervisis, Associate Professor, Oncology
Dr. Michael Childress, Professor, Comparative Oncology
Background
Lymphoma is one of the most common cancers in dogs, and while chemotherapy can often put the disease into remission, it is rarely curative. This study is investigating whether a noninvasive technology, High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound (HIFU), can safely destroy part of a cancerous lymph node and stimulate the immune system to help fight the cancer throughout the body.
HIFU uses precisely focused ultrasound energy to generate heat that kills cancer cells within a targeted region, without surgery or radiation. Beyond directly killing tumor cells, this process may release tumor antigens and danger signals, "waking up" the immune system to recognize and attack lymphoma cells wherever they are.
In this trial, we will treat one enlarged lymph node with HIFU in dogs who have not yet received chemotherapy. We will then carefully analyze changes in the treated lymph node, an untreated lymph node, and the blood to see if the immune system is activated. All dogs will then receive a full course of standard CHOP chemotherapy at Purdue.
The potential benefits for participating dogs include receiving an innovative treatment at no cost, which may improve the effectiveness of chemotherapy and potentially help the immune system keep the cancer under control longer. There are no placebos in this trial.
Eligibility for Dogs to Participate in the Study
Be at least 1 year old and weigh over 8 kg (~18 lb)
Have an untreated, newly confirmed diagnosis of intermediate or large-cell, multicentric lymphoma (B or T-cell)
Have not received any chemotherapy, corticosteroids, or other anti-cancer treatment in the past 3 weeks (2 weeks for steroids)
Be healthy enough for sedation/anesthesia
Have completed full clinical staging (physical exam, lab work, imaging, and lymph node biopsy)
Have no other serious life-limiting diseases
Exclusion Criteria
Small-cell lymphoma or other round cell tumors
Stage V lymphoma (bone marrow or blood involvement) or extranodal lymphoma
Significant liver or kidney dysfunction
Poor overall performance status (VCOG > 2)
What is involved for the dog/dog owner?
Screening and Baseline Testing:
Owners will first meet with our oncology team to discuss standard treatment options. If interested in the trial, dogs will undergo:
Physical exam, CBC, chemistry, urinalysis
Thoracic radiographs and abdominal ultrasound
Lymph node biopsy (histopathology, immunohistochemistry, flow cytometry)
Clonality testing (PARR)
Study Procedures:
Day 0 (Baseline Sampling):
Needle biopsy of a lymph node on the opposite side of the biopsied lymph node
Blood draw for extracellular vesicle (EV) analysis
HIFU Treatment:
Within 1-7 days of baseline sampling, a portion of the target lymph node will be thermally ablated using the Theraclion Echopulse HIFU system under sedation.
Post-Treatment Sampling:
5-7 days after HIFU: repeat needle biopsies of treated and untreated lymph nodes and blood collection
Chemotherapy:
CHOP-based UW-25 protocol will begin immediately after post-HIFU sampling and continue for 25 weeks
Follow-Up:
Regular rechecks during chemotherapy for monitoring bloodwork and treatment response
Long-term monitoring until relapse
Financial Support
Once enrolled, the following will be provided at no cost:
The HIFU procedure, including sedation/anesthesia
All biopsies, blood tests, and lab work required by the study
A $2,000 credit toward the cost of the CHOP chemotherapy protocol
Up to $2,000 in additional support for managing any side effects linked to HIFU, or to be applied toward CHOP therapy
Reduced pricing ("research rate") for all other treatments and follow-up visits
Owners will be responsible for costs related to:
Initial diagnostic workup prior to enrollment
Any unrelated to HIFU medical care
Emergency visits due to HIFU

H-FIRE Liver Cancer Study
Principal Investigators
Dr. Nick Dervisis, Associate Professor, Oncology
Study Overview
This clinical trial is evaluating the safety and immune effects of High-Frequency Irreversible Electroporation (H-FIRE) for dogs diagnosed with liver cancer. While surgical removal of liver tumors can lead to excellent outcomes in selected cases, dogs with non-resectable or advanced disease currently have very limited treatment options and poor prognosis. H-FIRE is a novel, image-guided, non-thermal tumor ablation technology that delivers high-frequency electrical pulses to create microscopic pores in cancer cell membranes, leading to tumor cell death and potential immune activation.
Purpose of the Study
The goals of this study are to evaluate the safety and feasibility of H-FIRE in dogs with liver cancer, measure local and systemic immune responses after H-FIRE treatment, analyze tumor biopsies, blood immune cells, and cytokines before and after treatment, and determine whether a single H-FIRE treatment can stimulate a meaningful anti-tumor immune response.
Eligibility - Inclusion Criteria
Before enrollment, standard diagnostic testing is required, including:
Complete physical examination
Bloodwork (CBC and chemistry)
Urinalysis
Contrast CT scan of the chest and abdomen (under anesthesia or sedation)
Ultrasound-guided liver tumor biopsy
Dogs may qualify if:
One or more liver tumors are identified
Tumors are amenable to surgical resection
The dog is a suitable candidate for anesthesia and surgery
The owner has reviewed all standard-of-care options and elects to participate
Eligibility - Exclusion Criteria
Dogs are not eligible if they have:
Severe systemic illness that prevents safe anesthesia or surgery
Coagulation disorders that prevent biopsy or electroporation
Medical conditions that substantially increase anesthetic risk
Owner declines surgical tumor removal following H-FIRE
What Participation Involves
H-FIRE Treatment:
The H-FIRE procedure is performed under general anesthesia and guided by ultrasound. One or more needle electrodes are placed through a 1-2 mm skin opening into the tumor. Electrical pulses are delivered in microsecond bursts. Total treatment time is typically under 30 minutes.
Surgery (5-7 Days Later):
Surgical removal of the liver tumor under general anesthesia with a CT scan obtained immediately before surgery.
Follow-Up:
Dogs return at 2 weeks post-surgery for physical examination and suture removal. Additional diagnostics may be performed if medically indicated.
Risks and Side Effects
H-FIRE is an experimental therapy and is not part of standard veterinary care. Potential risks include fever, tumor inflammation, tumor-site discomfort, systemic inflammation, severe infection, and death. Diagnostic and anesthesia risks include bruising, inflammation, infection, anesthetic reactions, cardiopulmonary complications, and rare death.
Potential Benefits
Your dog may or may not directly benefit. Potential benefits include partial financial support for treatment, access to a novel tumor-targeted therapy, possible local tumor destruction, possible immune activation, and contribution to research benefiting both dogs and humans.
Alternatives to Participation
Alternatives include surgery alone, palliative medical management, no treatment, or euthanasia when medically appropriate.
One-Sentence Financial Summary
The study provides a $2,000 surgical credit and covers all H-FIRE, recheck, and post H-FIRE CT costs; owners remain responsible for remaining surgical fees, complications, and unrelated medical care.
Costs and Compensation
Covered by the Study:
$2,000 credit toward surgical resection
100% of H-FIRE procedure costs (anesthesia, electrodes, treatment delivery, side-effect management)
100% of post-H-FIRE CT imaging
100% of recheck visit costs
Owner Responsibility:
Remaining surgical costs beyond the $2,000 credit
Any medical complications unrelated to H-FIRE therapy
Any medical care not required by the study
Any unrelated medical expenses
Typical surgical cost at Purdue ranges between $4,000-$8,000 depending on tumor location and surgical complexity.
Voluntary Participation and Withdrawal
Participation is entirely voluntary. Owners may withdraw their dog from the study at any time without affecting access to standard care. Dogs may also be withdrawn for medical or safety reasons. Samples collected before withdrawal may still be used unless the owner requests otherwise.
Confidentiality
All study data are confidential. Published results will not include identifying information. Research records are stored securely and accessible only to authorized personnel.

title: Transarterial embolization for canine nasal tumors
current_primary_text:
Novel Treatment for Nasal Tumors
STATUS: Active - Recruiting
Nasal tumors can cause severe nasal bleeding or discharge and difficulty breathing. These tumors often aggressively spread throughout the tissues of the nasal cavity and into the surrounding organs, including the eye and brain. Radiation therapy is the treatment of choice for nasal tumors in dogs; however, radiation therapy isn't often good for long-term control of the tumor. An another treatment option is transarterial embolization, or TAE, which involves the delivery of a mechanical “clot” to the main arteries supplying blood to the tissues of the nasal cavity with the goal of eliminating the blood supply of the tumor and decreasing tumor size.

The purposes of this study are to 1) describe TAE in dogs with naturally-occurring nasal cancer, 2) evaluate the effect that nasal TAE has on the tumor, and 3) evaluate the effect that nasal TAE has on the values measured by positron emission tomography (PET) scanning.
INVESTIGATOR: Dr. Bill Culp, Professor

title: Transarterial embolization or chemoembolization for non-resectable canine liver tumors
current_primary_text:
Assessing a new technique to shrink liver tumors in dogs
STATUS: Active - Recruiting
When liver tumors in dogs cannot be removed with surgery, treatment options are limited or non-existent. In humans, one of the standard treatments for those cases is transarterial chemoembolization (TACE), which eliminates the blood supply of the tumor and may decrease tumor size. The objectives of this study are to 1) describe the procedure of TACE  using a novel treatment agent in a group of dogs with naturally-occurring liver cancer, and 2) evaluate the effect that liver TACE has on clinical signs, size and viability of the tumor.

Demonstrating the feasibility and efficacy of liver TACE to improve clinical signs and decrease tumor size and volume can significantly advance our treatment of this difficult disease process, as current treatment options are limited and lack efficacy. Additionally, liver TACE is minimally invasive and provides many potential advantages over traditional surgical therapies.

The School of Veterinary Science has several clinical trials and research studies seeking volunteers and input from the public.
Each trial or research study has varying requirements in regards to the assistance the investigators are requiring. We invite you to take a look at the current trials listed below to see if you can contribute.
Please note that all clinical trials and research have animal ethics and/or human ethics approvals, participation is voluntary and any participants can be removed from a trial at any time.
Dog bone cancer vaccine trial
We are looking for pet dogs diagnosed with cancer to test an experimental vaccine. The clinical research trial is for dogs recently diagnosed with canine appendicular osteosarcoma, a common bone tumour that affects 10,000 dogs a year globally. In this trial, our researchers will assess two vaccine formulations. To be eligible, dogs need to have been diagnosed with appendicular osteosarcoma of long bones of the limbs with no evidence of metastasis, or cancer spread, based on a physical exam and radiographs. Dogs can be any breed but must be proceeding to surgery to treat their cancer. Read more
about these trials
.

Dr José Granados Soler
.
Cattle with lantana camara toxicity
We are looking for cattle that are naturally intoxicated with lantana camara.  Lantana is a common toxic plant in Queensland. We are searching for prognostic indicators of intoxicated cattle to better identify cattle that will survive. If you have cattle that are showing signs of photosensitization and have access to lantana, we would like to include them in the study. Photosensitization will present as thickened or “crusty” skin that is more firm that normal.  It occurs commonly in the white skinned areas, ears, nose and rear legs, but can occur anywhere on the body. Involvement in the study will consist of the cost of the campus vet mileage at $1.81/km roundtrip and the cost of the pharmaceuticals needed to treat. Blood, urine physical examination data, and pictures will be collected from the diseased animal and a healthy individual from the same paddock. Standard therapy will be activated charcoal by mouth and oxytetracycline injectable. The examination, pharmaceutical administration, and veterinary advice will be free.  We are searching for prognostic indicators of intoxicated cattle to better identify cattle that will survive.

title: Personalized mRNA therapeutic cancer vaccine for canine mast cell tumor

Why we are running this trial
From Rosie’s story to a future for more dogs.
Rosie
The first dog treated with a personalised neoantigen vaccine.
It began with Rosie. Her experience with a personalised neoantigen vaccine encouraged Paul to explore how this approach could one day be made available to every dog with cancer.
Before an approach like this can become broadly available, we must study it carefully and support it by evidence for review by the relevant veterinary regulators. This clinical trial is an important step in that process, helping us learn from participating dogs and understand the vaccine more fully.
Read Rosie’s personalised mRNA cancer-vaccine story  →
Who can register
If your dog has cancer and is currently in Australia, you’re welcome to register your interest. Our team will check whether your dog may be eligible for this trial.
Register your interest  →
About the trial
What this trial is looking at
The trial will investigate a personalised mRNA vaccine approach for dogs with mast cell cancer. Tell us about your dog and our team will help determine whether they may be eligible for screening.
Who can register
Dogs diagnosed with mast cell cancer who are based in, or able to travel within, Australia.
Every case is reviewed individually
The trial approach
A therapeutic mRNA vaccine designed from each dog’s own tumour and blood samples, intended to work alongside—not replace—existing care.
Personalised to each dog
What screening involves
We help coordinate records, screening, sample logistics and updates, working with the trial team and your treating veterinarian.
A named team stays in touch

How to register your interest.
You don’t need to have every record ready before registering your interest. Start with what you know and we’ll help with the rest.

Register your interest

The authorised study team and treating veterinarian assess potential eligibility. If your dog may proceed, you’ll receive the approved trial information and consent discussion before deciding.

ReachGlio: nuevo ensayo clínico para perros con glioma de alto grado
17 septiembre, 2026
Hospital Veterinario Puchol
Neurologia
El Hospital Veterinario Puchol ha iniciado el reclutamiento de pacientes para
ReachGlio, un Ensayo Clínico Veterinario dirigido a perros con diagnóstico presuntivo de glioma de alto grado
, uno de los tumores cerebrales más complejos en neurología y oncología veterinaria.
El estudio ha sido autorizado por la
Agencia Española de Medicamentos y Productos Sanitarios (AEMPS)
y está financiado en el marco de la convocatoria europea
TRANSCAN-3
, orientada a impulsar la investigación traslacional en cáncer.
El Ensayo Clínico Veterinario se desarrollará en el
Hospital Veterinario Puchol
, en el marco de un proyecto de investigación promovido por la Unidad de Neurooncología del Instituto de Salud Carlos III, y coordinado por la Universidad Camilo José Cela.
Más allá de evaluar una nueva estrategia terapéutica en el contexto de un ensayo clínico, ReachGlio busca responder a una pregunta especialmente relevante en neurooncología:
¿Podemos conseguir que los tratamientos antitumorales lleguen de forma más eficaz a las células tumoradas en el cerebro?
Isidro Mateo y Rafaela Draque en intervención quirúrgica (Servicio de Neurología HV Puchol)
Glioma en perros: uno de los grandes retos de la neurología veterinaria
Los gliomas son tumores primarios del sistema nervioso central que se originan a partir de células de estirpe glial. Dentro de este grupo se incluyen fundamentalmente a los oligodendrogliomas y los astrocitomas.
Aparecen principalmente en perros adultos o geriátricos y se ha descrito una mayor predisposición en determinadas razas, especialmente entre las braquicéfalas.
Si nos preguntamos cuales son los síntomas de un tumor cerebral en un perro, estos dependen de la localización y extensión del tumor. Entre las manifestaciones que pueden aparecer se encuentran:
crisis epilépticas de nueva aparición;
cambios de comportamiento;
alteraciones del nivel de consciencia;
desorientación;
alteraciones de la marcha;
déficits neurológicos focales.
Glioma presente en perros y humanos
En un perro adulto, la aparición de una primera crisis epiléptica o de otros signos neurológicos progresivos puede justificar una valoración neurológica especializada y la realización de pruebas de diagnóstico por imagen, entre ellas la resonancia magnética cerebral.
El papel de la resonancia magnética
La
resonancia magnética cerebral en perros
es una herramienta fundamental para identificar y caracterizar una masa intracraneal y, en combinación con la evaluación clínica, permite establecer un diagnóstico diferencial muy específico de glioma de alto grado.
Sin embargo, la clasificación definitiva del tumor requiere su estudio histopatológico.
Resonancia magnética cerebral compatible con glioma
La barrera hematoencefálica: cuando el propio cerebro dificulta el tratamiento
Uno de los principales desafíos del tratamiento farmacológico del tumor cerebral en perros es la
barrera hematoencefálica
.
Se trata de un sistema de protección esencial que regula de manera muy estricta el paso de determinadas sustancias desde la sangre hacia el tejido nervioso.
Esa protección, imprescindible para el funcionamiento normal del cerebro, supone también un desafío terapéutico: algunos medicamentos pueden tener dificultades para alcanzar concentraciones terapéuticas en los tumores cerebrales o gliomas caninos.
Además, ésta barrera hematoencefálica no es uniforme en todo el tumor, algunas zonas pueden ser más permeables, mientras que otras continúan limitando significativamente la entrada de determinados tratamientos.
Por tanto, conseguir que un fármaco llegue al cerebro no significa necesariamente que alcance de manera suficiente todas las áreas relevantes del tumor.
Este es precisamente uno de los retos que investiga ReachGlio.
¿Qué estudia exactamente ReachGlio?
El Ensayo Clínico Veterinario evaluará una estrategia basada en la administración de
SNGR-TNF en combinación con temozolomida
.
Según el protocolo del estudio, SNGR-TNF es un agente dirigido a la vasculatura tumoral cuya finalidad es inducir una modificación transitoria y controlada de la barrera hematoencefálica.
El objetivo es estudiar si esta modificación puede favorecer una mayor penetración de la temozolomida, el principal quimioterápico utilizado para el tratamiento de glioma canino y humano de alto grado.
Por tanto, ReachGlio no evalúa únicamente un nuevo esquema de tratamiento. Su planteamiento científico consiste en estudiar si es posible
modificar temporalmente las condiciones de acceso al tumor para favorecer la exposición al fármaco
.
Se trata de un ensayo piloto de naturaleza exploratoria, por lo que uno de sus principales objetivos será obtener información sobre farmacodinamia, tolerabilidad y seguridad que permita orientar futuras fases de investigación.
Un diseño con ajuste dinámico de dosis
Otro de los aspectos relevantes del estudio es su diseño.
ReachGlio utilizará un modelo secuencial con
ajuste dinámico de dosis
, en el que las decisiones se tomarán teniendo en cuenta parámetros de seguridad y biomarcadores farmacodinámicos.
Este planteamiento permite incorporar la información obtenida progresivamente durante el ensayo y ajustar la dosis de acuerdo con los criterios de seguridad y los datos farmacodinámicos establecidos en el protocolo.
La autorización de la AEMPS implica además que el estudio debe desarrollarse bajo un protocolo previamente definido, con requisitos específicos de seguridad, seguimiento, documentación y bienestar animal.
¿Qué perros pueden ser candidatos?
ReachGlio está dirigido a
perros con diagnóstico presuntivo de glioma de alto grado y un peso corporal igual o superior a 7 kg
, que además cumplan los criterios establecidos en el protocolo del estudio.
La identificación de un posible candidato comienza mucho antes de la inclusión en el estudio.
El papel del veterinario generalista y del veterinario remitente resulta especialmente importante ante pacientes que presentan signos compatibles con enfermedad prosencefálica, especialmente:
crisis epilépticas de nueva aparición en un perro adulto
cambios conductuales
alteración del estado mental
déficits neurológicos focales
Tras la evaluación neurológica y las pruebas de diagnóstico por imagen correspondientes, los pacientes que presenten hallazgos compatibles con los criterios iniciales podrán ser valorados individualmente para estudiar su posible inclusión en el estudio.
Imagen histológica de tejido tumoral compatible con glioma.
¿Qué implica participar en ReachGlio?
Los perros incluidos recibirán
seis ciclos de tratamiento, con un intervalo de 21 días entre cada ciclo
.
El protocolo contempla visitas al Hospital Veterinario Puchol para la administración intravenosa del tratamiento y su monitorización, junto con medicación oral en domicilio.
El seguimiento incluirá:
evaluaciones neurológicas periódicas;
controles analíticos;
resonancias magnéticas con contraste para valoración de los cambios en el tumor;
monitorización de posibles efectos adversos;
y valoración de la evolución de la lesión.
El protocolo contempla también la confirmación histopatológica post mortem del tumor, realizada por laboratorios especializados.
Glioma cerebral observado en necropsia.
Aunque este aspecto requiere una comunicación especialmente sensible con las familias, permite obtener información muy valiosa para la investigación, ya que hace posible relacionar los hallazgos de la resonancia magnética y la evolución clínica con las características histológicas del tumor. Esta información es imprescindible para comprender mejor la enfermedad y, particularmente, para interpretar los resultados obtenidos durante el ensayo.
El Hospital Veterinario Puchol desarrollará la fase clínica veterinaria
La incorporación del Hospital Veterinario Puchol al proyecto permitirá trasladar esta investigación al contexto clínico, trabajando con pacientes caninos con tumores que aparecen de forma espontánea, dentro de un entorno clínico especializado y bajo un protocolo específicamente autorizado.
El hospital será el centro encargado de desarrollar el ensayo clínico, con participación de su
Servicio de Neurología
y de los recursos necesarios para la evaluación clínica, el diagnóstico por imagen, la administración del tratamiento y el seguimiento de los pacientes.
Los procedimientos específicamente contemplados dentro del protocolo de investigación, incluyendo el tratamiento, las resonancias de seguimiento y las analíticas vinculadas al estudio, están financiados en el marco de TRANSCAN-3 y no supondrán un coste adicional para los propietarios.
Sin embargo, el principal valor de este proyecto no es económico.
ReachGlio representa la posibilidad de que determinados pacientes con una enfermedad neurológica grave accedan a una estrategia terapéutica experimental única dentro de un Ensayo Clínico regulado, protocolizado y estrechamente monitorizado, pudiéndose beneficiar de las nuevas oportunidades terapéuticas que ofrecen moléculas actualmente en desarrollo
Y representa también algo esencial para el futuro de la medicina veterinaria:
seguir generando evidencia allí donde todavía existen preguntas sin respuesta
.
Información para veterinarios
El reclutamiento de pacientes comenzó el
1 de septiembre de 2026
.
Los veterinarios que atiendan a un perro con una lesión intracraneal compatible con un glioma de alto grado pueden contactar con el Hospital Veterinario Puchol para valorar conjuntamente si el paciente cumple inicialmente los criterios necesarios para ser considerado candidato al ensayo.
La puesta en marcha de ReachGlio supone un nuevo paso en el compromiso del Hospital Veterinario Puchol con una medicina basada en la
especialización, el rigor científico, la innovación y la investigación clínica
, especialmente en enfermedades complejas en las que todavía es necesario seguir avanzando.

title: Single-fraction radiation therapy for canine transmissible venereal tumor
current_primary_text:
Single Radiation Treatment for Dogs with Transmissible Venereal Tumor
STATUS: Active - Recruiting
Canine transmissible venereal tumor (TVT) is an infectious cancer that can be spread between dogs, often through grooming behaviors or sexual contact. This cancer can be found worldwide, but is most common in Central and South America, Africa, and Asia. In the United States, this cancer is most commonly seen in animals rescued from other parts of the world, or in free-roaming pets in very remote areas.
Treatment for this cancer involves once-weekly injections of chemotherapy, which are given until the cancer is resolved. For patients who cannot undergo this chemotherapy treatment, finding alternate therapies can be invaluable. We know that this cancer responds well to older forms of radiation therapy; however, we aim to determine if a single treatment with modernized radiation can provide similar treatment outcomes with fewer visits compared to chemotherapy.

title: Actionable targeted therapies after amputation or for metastatic canine osteosarcoma
current_primary_text:
Defining Actionable Targets for Osteosarcoma
< BACK TO ALL
					CLINICAL-TRIALS
Recruiting
Dog
Oncology
Osteosarcoma represents a challenging disease to treat in both dogs and humans. In dogs with osteosarcoma, despite 30 years of effort and multiple clinical studies, the median survival time after amputation of the affected leg followed by carboplatin chemotherapy remains 11 months; only 25% of dogs will live to 2 years. With advances in technology, we now have a much better understanding of the underlying genetic changes that help drive osteosarcoma growth. The purpose of this study is to use this information and determine whether specific drugs that target key defects in osteosarcoma cells are effective for preventing the development of tumor spread (metastasis) following amputation of the affected limb. We will be testing three different drugs that target individual proteins/pathways known to be abnormal in osteosarcoma. These are 1) olaparib, a drug that targets a protein called PARP which is most effective in cells that have defective DNA repair which is common in osteosarcoma; 2) temozolomide, a chemotherapy drug that targets cells with defective DNA repair; and 3) VLS-1488, a drug that targets cells with defective Rb protein, a common finding in osteosarcoma. In the current study, we will be testing how well each of these drugs work in dogs after the tumor has been removed, instead of using carboplatin chemotherapy.
Group A: Dogs with newly diagnosed OS will receive treatment with the drug of interest prior to amputation (tumor removal) and then continue on this treatment after tumor removal in place of standard chemotherapy.
Group B: Dogs that have failed treatment (either standard of care therapy [amputation + carboplatin chemotherapy] or novel drug therapy [amputation + novel drug]) and have developed metastasis will receive the drug(s) of interest until progression of disease is noted.
Inclusion Criteria
Eligibility for Group A:
Presumptive diagnosis of Osteosarcoma in a limb bone based on cytology or biopsy
No obvious evidence of tumor spread based on chest x-rays or CT scan
No concurrent health conditions (heart, kidney, liver disease, among others) that may interfere with either treatment or overall survival
Weigh at least 15 kg
No clinically significant abnormalities on baseline bloodwork (CBC/chemistry).
No prior diagnosis of a malignant tumor that is likely to impact overall survival.
Not receiving any other small molecule therapies (i.e., oclacitinib, etc.) that may interfere with the planned drug treatments.
Eligibility for Group B:
Prior diagnosis of OS with amputation and either carboplatin chemotherapy or study drug therapy
Metastasis to the lungs, skin/subcutaneous tissue and/or abdomen with no evidence of bone metastasis
No concurrent health conditions (heart, kidney, liver disease, among others) that may interfere with either treatment or overall survival.
Weigh at least 15 kg
No clinically significant abnormalities on baseline bloodwork (CBC/chemistry).
No prior diagnosis of a malignant tumor that is likely to impact overall survival.
Not receiving any other small molecule therapies (i.e., oclacitinib, etc.) that may interfere with the planned drug treatments.
Have a life expectancy of at least 1 month
Exclusion Criteria
Dogs weighing less than 15 kg (33 pounds)
Concurrent health conditions (heart, kidney, liver disease, among others) that may interfere with either treatment or overall survival.
Receiving any other small molecule therapies (i.e., oclacitinib, etc.) that may interfere with the planned drug treatments.
Significant kidney, heart, or liver disease and abnormalities on a complete blood count.
Client Benefits
For participation in the clinical study, all costs associated with study screening are covered and you will receive a $1500 credit toward amputation of your dog’s leg. Additionally, all costs associated with treatment post-amputation will be covered, including those associated with any potential side effects. Treatment of conditions unrelated to the study (i.e., ear infection) are not covered by the study.
Sample or Data Requirements
Baseline screening tests include routine bloodwork (complete blood count, chemistry panel), a urine exam, and whole body CT exam. Once enrolled in the study, your dog will have a tumor biopsy performed under sedation (this is not general anesthesia). Your dog will then receive 6 days of the oral study drug. Your dog will return to the hospital on day 7, where we will administer the study drug, then take samples of blood at 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8 hours after drug to measure blood levels of the drug. The following day, your dog will undergo limb amputation. Your dog will return to the clinic 7 days post-amputation for a recheck exam and to restart the study drug. We will then see your dog monthly post amputation for a physical exam and routine bloodwork, with a whole-body CT scan performed under sedation every 2 months to monitor for tumor spread. Throughout the study, we will take blood samples from your dog to investigate potential biomarkers that could indicate response or resistance to treatment and help determine which osteosarcoma subtypes are more likely to respond to the study drug. The maximum blood volume drawn at any study visit is 40 ml, (2 tablespoons + 2 teaspoons). We will also do two buccal swabs on the first visit, which are used to collect normal DNA from the mouth by rotating a swab in the cheek pouch for 30-60 seconds.
Contact Information
For questions regarding the clinical trial, please email
clinicaltrials@tufts.edu
.

Referring Physician Questionnaire
If you believe you have a patient who is eligible for this clinical trial study or you would like additional information from the Clinical Trials Office, complete a referring physician questionnaire.

慢性腸症罹患犬に対する乳酸菌およびオリゴ糖の有効性に関する臨床試験
犬の慢性腸症は食欲不振、嘔吐、下痢、体重減少などの症状を慢性的に引き起こす病気であり、治療により良化する症例がいる一方でさまざまな治療を行っても良化しない症例もいます。
慢性消化器症状を呈している犬では、免疫バランスや腸内フローラが乱れていることが多くの研究から明らかにされています。一方、乳酸菌は免疫バランスを整え、またオリゴ糖はビフィズス菌などの善玉菌を増やし、腸内フローラを改善する作用が確認されています。そこで、慢性腸症の中で投薬治療を必要としない、症状が比較的軽度の犬を対象に、下痢などの慢性症状に対する乳酸菌とオリゴ糖の有効性を評価するために臨床試験を実施しています。

犬猫の固形腫瘍に対するがんオルガノイドスクリーニング検査に基づく分子標的薬投与の安全性と有効性検証のための臨床試験
根治的な外科手術の困難な犬猫の転移性・浸潤性の固形腫瘍症例に対する効果的な標準治療は乏しいのが現状です。医学領域のがん治療では、そのような転移性・浸潤性の固形腫瘍症例に対して、分子標的薬が用いられ、高い治療効果が得られています。しかし、獣医学領域では各腫瘍に対する分子標的薬の有効性データが乏しく、適応は一部の腫瘍(例：肥満細胞腫におけるトセラニブなど)に限られています。
そこで、犬猫の固形腫瘍に対して症例ごとに有効な分子標的薬を特定し、パーソナライズ治療を行うためのがんオルガノイドスクリーニング検査を開発しました(池田ら,世界獣医がん学会,2024)。本検査では、犬猫症例より生検または外科手術により採材した腫瘍組織を用いて、スクリーニング検査を実施し、有効な分子標的薬の候補を同定します。
本臨床試験では、対象症例ごとにがんオルガノイドスクリーニング検査を実施し、有効性の期待される分子標的薬の投与を行い、その有効性と安全性を検証します。本臨床試験は、2025年6月に東京大学附属動物医療センター臨床試験委員会で承認を受けました。
対象
根治的な標準治療の確立されていない犬猫の固形腫瘍症例(具体的な腫瘍種の例としてはリンパ腫や白血病などの血液腫瘍を除く、上皮系腫瘍(扁平上皮癌、腺癌、移行上皮癌、未分化癌など)、非上皮系腫瘍(軟部組織肉腫(線維肉腫、脂肪肉腫、平滑筋肉腫、横紋筋肉腫、血管肉腫、末梢神経鞘腫、滑膜肉腫など)、悪性黒色腫、中皮腫、肥満細胞腫など)、神経内分泌腫瘍(インスリノーマ、ガストリノーマ、ケモデクトーマ、脳腫瘍など)など) (計測可能な標的病変を有すること)

ネコの移行上皮癌に対するラパチニブの獣医師主導臨床試験
ネコの移行上皮癌は尿路に発生する悪性腫瘍です。ネコでの発生頻度はまれですが、悪性度が高く、予後が悪いことが知られています。外科手術により癌組織をすべて摘出することができれば根治となりますが、手術を行っても再発や転移を起こすことがあります。また、既に転移のある症例に対して根治目的の手術はできません。そのため内科療法が重要となりますが、現在のところ有効な薬剤は確立されていません。
私たちはこれまでの研究で、ネコの移行上皮癌の治療標的としてHER2という分子を発見しました。そこでHER2に対する分子標的薬であるラパチニブ（商品名タイケルブ®）の有効性と安全性を調べるために臨床試験を実施しています。この試験は2023年12月に東京大学附属動物医療センター臨床試験委員会で承認を受けました。ご協力いただける方は上記連絡先（東京大学附属動物医療センター受付）にご連絡ください。

犬の膀胱・尿道移行上皮癌および前立腺癌に対する臨床試験
本臨床試験は目標症例数に達したため、2021年12月1日をもって終了することとなりました。ご参加くださった飼い主さま、ご紹介いただいた先生方、誠にありがとうございました。臨床試験は終了となりますが、新薬は実費であれば使用できますので、移行上皮癌・前立腺癌でお困りの場合は是非ご相談ください。
詳細につきましては
担当獣医師のホームページ
をご確認ください。
犬の膀胱・尿道移行上皮癌および前立腺癌は、尿路に発生する悪性腫瘍です。外科手術により癌組織をすべて摘出することができれば根治となりますが、犬の移行上皮癌や前立腺癌は悪性度が高く、手術を行っても再発や転移を起こしてしまうことがあります。また既に転移のある症例に対して、根治目的の手術は不適応となります。そのため内科療法が重要となりますが、現在のところ有効な薬剤は確立されていません。
これまでの研究により、犬の移行上皮癌や前立腺の発症・悪化に関わるメカニズムを解析したところ、治療のターゲットとなりうる分子を発見しました。そこで現在、その分子に特異的に作用する薬剤を用いて、臨床試験を実施しています。この臨床試験は、2017年7月に東京大学附属動物医療センター治験委員会で承認を受けました。

犬の膀胱癌に対するIDO1阻害剤の臨床試験

犬の固形腫瘍に対する高分子型抗癌剤の臨床試験
一般に、限局性の固形腫瘍に対する第一選択は外科手術ですが、手術で取りきることが難しいほどに進行してしまった症例や全身に転移しやすい腫瘍に罹患した症例では、外科手術に加えて、抗癌剤や放射線療法が適用となります。しかし、いずれの治療法も治療効果が乏しく、有効な治療法がないことが多いのが現状です。
固形腫瘍の血管は特有の血管壁の大きな隙間が存在し、薬剤を高分子化しサイズを大きくすることで、その隙間より薬剤が漏れ出し蓄積しやすくなるEPR(Enhanced Permeability and Retention)効果があります(Matumura Y, Maeda H, Can Res, 1986)。 EPR効果を利用することで、健康な臓器に比べ腫瘍組織に多くの薬剤を集積させられます。そこで、ピラルビシンと呼ばれる抗癌剤と高分子ポリマーを結合させた高分子型抗癌剤を開発し、マウスモデルにおいて低分子型抗癌剤(普段用いられるタイプの抗癌剤)に勝る抗腫瘍効果が得られることを発見しました(Nakamura H, Maeda H, J Control Release, 2014)。
外科系診療科では、2021年10月に東京大学附属動物医療センター治験委員会で承認を受け、高分子型抗癌剤を用いた臨床試験を行なっています。
対象
外科手術による根治的切除不能あるいは転移病変を有する悪性固形腫瘍のうち、放射線や抗癌剤などその他の有効な治療法が無い症例
(脳腫瘍、末梢神経鞘腫、扁平上皮癌、線維肉腫、悪性黒色腫、甲状腺癌、肺癌、肝臓癌、膵臓癌、胃癌、腸腺癌、消化管間質腫瘍、 副腎腫瘍、腎癌、尿路上皮癌、肛門嚢腺癌、乳癌、骨肉腫、血管肉腫、肥満細胞種、組織球性肉腫などのうち、標準治療のの有効性が期待されない、または耐性となった症例)

お知らせとお詫び
2016年、当院にて実施した臨床試験*1を受けた猫のご家族からのご指摘により、この臨床試験が不適切に実施されていたことが判明しました。このことを反省し、再発防止のために新たな規約を制定することにしました。臨床試験は動物たちに新しい治療法などを試みるもので、有効性が期待される反面、効果がないことや健康上のリスクを伴うことがあります。臨床試験への参加には通常条件がありますが、実施する際には動物やご家族さまの権利と安全への配慮を最優先に考える必要があります。また、不利益やリスクを十分に説明し、ご家族さまの自由意志で試験にご参加いただくことが原則です。従来の治療法では助けられなかった動物たちに、救いの手となる診断法や治療法をみつけられるように今後とも努力してまいります。
*1) 2016年に当院で実施した慢性腎臓病のネコを対象にした獣医師主導の臨床試験（治験として参加者を募集）で重大な過ちがありました。
本来は対象とならない高齢のネコに対して臨床試験が行われた。
試験に参加していただく際、副作用の説明が適切でない状況で臨床試験への参加が促された。
使用した薬剤の副作用リスクの評価が不十分で、結果として一過性ではあるが重度の肝障害が生じた。
試験中に発生した肝障害がご家族に対して知らされることなく、試験が継続された。
ご参加いただいた方には、大変ご心痛、ご迷惑をおかけしましたことをお詫び申し上げます。当該臨床試験は終了しており、同じ内容で試験を受けた方、有害事象がみられた方にはすでに連絡済みですが、臨床試験を受けられた方でご心配な方はメールでご連絡ください。
